one_liner: Header-only C++20 double-ended vector: std::vector's contiguous storage plus std::deque's fast front growth.
what_it_does: veque is a contiguous, allocator-aware sequence container that reserves slack at both ends of its buffer, so it supports push/pop/resize from the front as cheaply as from the back while staying array-compatible (pointer iteration, C APIs, gsl::span). It implements the full std::vector interface (constructors, assign, iterators, capacity) plus std::deque's push_front/emplace_front/pop_front, so it is a near drop-in replacement for either, selectable via a ResizeTraits template parameter that tunes preallocation and iterator-invalidation behavior.
how_it_is_fast: Unused capacity is kept on both sides of the live elements instead of only at the back, so front insertion/growth is amortized O(1) like std::deque instead of std::vector's O(n) full-buffer shift. Arbitrary-position insert/erase can shift elements toward whichever end (front or back) is closer, roughly halving the average number of elements moved compared to std::vector's always-shift-to-back behavior. A ResizeTraits policy (fast_resize_traits by default) controls this trade-off and lets callers dial down to std::vector-style behavior (vector_compatible_resize_traits, std_vector_traits, no_reserve_traits) when they need std::vector's iterator-invalidation guarantees instead.
when_to_use: Vector-like contiguous container that also needs frequent push_front/pop_front or resize_front, not just back growth
Insert/erase happen near either end of the sequence, not predominantly in the middle, so closest-side shifting pays off
C++20 codebase (concepts/ranges already required) that can take a single dependency-free header
Want tunable memory-vs-invalidation behavior per container instantiation via the ResizeTraits template parameter
when_not_to_use: Toolchain is pre-C++20 (header requires <concepts> and <ranges>); no C++14/17 build exists despite a README wishlist entry
Memory is tight: veque reserves slack at both front and back by default, so its footprint exceeds std::vector's at the same size()
Workload is back-growth-heavy: in the project's own benchmark veque was slower than std::deque on back growth (552,027 vs 342,218us) and front growth (30,739 vs 16,386us)

Code depends on std::vector's partial iterator-invalidation guarantees on insert/erase; the default fast_resize_traits invalidates all iterators/references on those ops (opt into vector_compatible_resize_traits to get std::vector's rules back, at the cost of the closest-side speedup)
Need std::vector<bool>'s bit-packed specialization; veque<bool> is explicitly not specialized
Project is small and thinly used (128 stars, ~10 forks, effectively one author) with a past heap-corruption bug in assign() (fixed 2023) — worth vetting before production use

integration.min_toolchain: C++20 (uses <concepts> and <ranges>); the benchmark's sample-output comment is labelled g++-9, which predates full <ranges> support, so that sample may be stale relative to current code
integration.platforms: not documented; no platform-specific code observed, standard C++20 only
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — matches std::vector's full API (and adds std::deque's front operations), but the default fast_resize_traits changes iterator/reference invalidation rules on insert/erase to always-invalidate; true std::vector-compatible invalidation requires switching to vector_compatible_resize_traits

gotchas: Default ResizeTraits (fast_resize_traits) invalidates ALL iterators and references on any insert/erase, unlike std::vector's partial invalidation — use vector_compatible_resize_traits for std::vector's guarantees
veque<bool> is not specialized/bit-packed, unlike std::vector<bool>
Closed issue #9 reported heap corruption after veque destruction, triggered via assign(); maintainer marked it fixed in a later release (2023-06-20) — pin a recent commit rather than an old tag
fast_resize_traits preallocates slack at both ends by default, so memory use is higher than std::vector even at equal size(); no_reserve_traits removes that at the cost of resize speed
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick veque over the catalogued siblings (plf::colony/hive, plf::list, eastl::vector, fast_vector) when you need std::vector's contiguous, ordered, drop-in-ish interface but also do real front-side growth (push_front/pop_front/resize_front): eastl::vector and fast_vector only optimize back-end std::vector operations, and plf::colony/plf::list trade away contiguous ordered storage entirely.
verified_claims_summary: In the project's own performance/main.cpp harness (g++-9 -O3, CPU/hardware unstated), veque totaled 2,492,954us across seven operations vs std::vector's 10,248,719us (~4.1x) and std::deque's 3,480,344us (~1.4x); the largest single gap was front growth, where std::vector's O(n)-per-op reallocation cost 6,685,217us vs veque's 30,739us (~217x), while veque itself was slower than std::deque on both front growth (30,739 vs 16,386us) and back growth (552,027 vs 342,218us) in the same run.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-15, BSL-1.0 license) but small and effectively single-author (128 stars, ~10 forks); a past heap-corruption bug in assign() was reported and fixed, so use a current commit rather than an old release.
